note: Class 12 Mathematics, Review 2 and Review 3 multiple-choice questions (no printed key in the page book). Each answer was worked out and checked; three printed options need a note (xv, Review 3 vi, vii, ix).

leaves.why: In $y = f(x)$ the variable $x$ is the one whose values are chosen freely (the input); $y$ depends on it.
$f(-3) = \dfrac{3(-3)^2 - 2}{3(-3) + 9} = \dfrac{25}{0}$: division by zero is not defined.
The denominator $3x + 9$ is zero only at $x = -3$, so the domain is every real number except $-3$.
The denominator $3x^2 + 9$ is positive for every real $x$, so no value of $x$ is excluded.
When $y$ is written directly in terms of $x$ as $y = f(x)$, the function is called explicit; an implicit function has $x$ and $y$ mixed in one equation.
Take $\ln$ of both sides of $5^x = 7$: $x \ln 5 = \ln 7$, so $x = \dfrac{\ln 7}{\ln 5}$.
$f(x) = \dfrac{2}{x^2 - 9}$ is not defined where $x^2 - 9 = 0$, i.e. at $x = \pm 3$, so it is discontinuous there.

leaves.answer: c) $\dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(-\dfrac{1 - x}{x - 1}\right)$ is the printed option closest to the answer $\dfrac{1}{2}\log\dfrac{1 + x}{1 - x}$ (the inverse of $\tanh x$); the printed option has $1 - x$ where $1 + x$ is needed.
leaves.why: Put $y = \dfrac{e^x - e^{-x}}{e^x + e^{-x}} = \dfrac{e^{2x} - 1}{e^{2x} + 1}$. Then $e^{2x}(1 - y) = 1 + y$, so $e^{2x} = \dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y}$ and $x = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\dfrac{1 + y}{1 - y} = \dfrac{1}{2}\log\left(-\dfrac{1 + y}{y - 1}\right)$. Options (a) and (b) have 2 in place of 1, and as printed option (c) gives $\log 1 = 0$ and option (d) a negative number inside the logarithm, so (c) must be read with $1 + x$ (a misprint in the book).
This is the definition of the derivative (limit of the difference quotient).
$h(t) = t^{3/2}$, so $h'(t) = \dfrac{3}{2}t^{1/2} = \dfrac{3}{2}\sqrt{t}$. Options (c) $\dfrac{3t}{2\sqrt{t}}$ and (d) $\dfrac{3t^2}{2\sqrt{t^3}}$ are the same value written differently.
Product rule: $\dfrac{d}{dx}(x\tan x) = \tan x + x\sec^2 x$. Option (d) $\tan x + x[1 + \tan^2 x]$ is the same, because $1 + \tan^2 x = \sec^2 x$.

The derivative of $\sec^{-1}x$ is $\dfrac{1}{|x|\sqrt{x^2 - 1}}$. The question prints $x^2 + 1$ under the root, a misprint for $x^2 - 1$: of the four options only $\sec^{-1}x$ has a derivative of this form.
